disclaimer: General first-response information only, NOT a diagnosis or a treatment plan. It has not yet been reviewed by a veterinarian: have a qualified vet or your national veterinary service review and localise it before field use. Never give medicines without a vet's instruction.
note: Single source for the offline app and for the LLM API's fallback when the language model is unavailable. mobile/src/data/diseases.json must be an exact copy (tests/test_advice_pack.py checks it). No drug names or doses on purpose.

diseases.label: lumpy_skin_disease
diseases.title: Lumpy skin disease (LSD)
signs: Firm, round, raised lumps (about 1-5 cm) on the skin, often over the head, neck, legs, udder and body
Fever, loss of appetite, drop in milk yield
Swollen lymph nodes; watery eye and nose discharge
Lumps can ulcerate and scab; swelling of the legs and brisket
do_now: Separate the animal from the herd and keep it away from other farms' animals
Do not move or sell animals; call your veterinarian or the animal-health authority at once: LSD is a reportable (notifiable) disease in most countries
Reduce biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks (they spread it): clean manure, remove standing water, use vet-approved repellents
Do not share needles, tools or water troughs between animals
Handle sick animals last and wash hands and boots afterwards
prevention: Vaccination through official programmes
Insect control and movement controls
Buy animals only from known healthy herds and quarantine new arrivals
diseases.see_vet: Treatment is supportive and decided by a vet (for example for secondary infections). Early reporting limits spread.

diseases.label: foot_and_mouth_disease
diseases.title: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
diseases.species: Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs (and other cloven-hoofed animals)
signs: Blisters and raw erosions on the tongue, gums, lips and muzzle
Blisters between the hooves and on the coronary band; lameness, reluctance to move
Drooling, smacking of the lips, loss of appetite, fever
Lesions on the teats; sharp fall in milk
do_now: Treat as an emergency: it spreads extremely fast. Call your veterinarian or the animal-health authority immediately
Isolate the animal and stop all movement of animals, people, vehicles and equipment on and off the farm
Do not take the animal to markets, shows or shared pasture
Disinfect boots, clothes and vehicles with a vet-approved disinfectant; keep visitors away
Keep feed and water for sick animals separate
prevention: Vaccination matched to the circulating virus type, through official programmes
Strict biosecurity and movement control; quarantine new animals
Report any suspicious case early: this is what protects neighbouring farms
diseases.see_vet: There is no specific cure; control is by official measures. Only a laboratory test can confirm FMD.

diseases.label: tick
diseases.title: Tick infestation
signs: Small round ticks attached to the skin, often in clusters around ears, udder, groin, tail base and between the legs
Skin irritation, hair loss, restlessness; heavy burdens cause anaemia and poor growth
Fever, pale gums, weakness or dark urine can point to a tick-borne disease
do_now: Remove ticks with a proper tick remover, pulling steadily; do not crush them or burn them on the animal
Ask a vet or animal-health worker which tick-control product is approved and safe locally, and follow the label
Check the whole herd, especially ears, udder and groin; keep pasture and housing tidy
If the animal has fever, weakness, pale gums or dark urine, call a vet the same day
prevention: Regular, vet-advised tick control and pasture management
Inspect animals routinely and after grazing in bush
diseases.see_vet: Tick-borne diseases need a vet's diagnosis and treatment.

diseases.label: wound_abscess
diseases.title: Wounds, injuries and abscesses
signs: Cuts, tears, swellings or abscesses; limping; blood or pus; flies around the area
Heat, pain, bad smell or swelling suggest infection
do_now: Restrain the animal calmly and safely; avoid being kicked or bitten
Control heavy bleeding with firm, clean pressure
Rinse the wound with plenty of clean water; keep flies off
Call a vet for deep, bleeding, infected, joint or hoof wounds, or any wound near the eyes; wounds can lead to tetanus, so ask the vet about protection
prevention: Remove sharp objects and fix fences and housing
Keep bedding and handling areas clean and dry
diseases.see_vet: A vet should decide on wound closure, antibiotics and pain relief.

diseases.label: mange_crusting
diseases.title: Mange / skin crusting
signs: Intense itching, rubbing, hair loss, thick crusts and scabs, often on the head, neck, flanks and base of the tail
Thickened wrinkled skin in long-standing cases; weight loss
do_now: Separate affected animals and avoid sharing brushes, ropes and housing
Ask a vet or animal-health worker for a skin scraping to confirm the cause and which treatment is approved locally
Wear gloves when handling and wash hands and clothes afterwards: some mange mites can cause itchy skin in people
Clean and disinfect housing and equipment
prevention: Quarantine and inspect new animals
Keep housing clean and not overcrowded
diseases.see_vet: Treatment depends on the mite and must follow the product label and veterinary advice.

diseases.label: ringworm_patch
diseases.title: Ringworm patches
signs: Round, grey-white, crusty, hairless patches, often on the head, around the eyes and on the neck
Usually little itching; spreads in crowded or damp housing
do_now: Separate affected animals; it spreads by contact and shared equipment
Wear gloves and wash hands well: ringworm spreads to people, especially children
Ask a vet which treatment is suitable and approved; do not scrape crusts off without gloves
Clean and disinfect housing and equipment; improve ventilation and dryness
prevention: Avoid crowding and damp housing
Isolate and inspect new animals
diseases.see_vet: Often clears by itself over months, but treatment limits spread.

diseases.label: eye_discharge_opacity
diseases.title: Eye discharge / cloudy eye (suspected pinkeye)
signs: Watery or pus-like eye discharge, squinting, light sensitivity
White or blue cloudiness of the eye surface; in severe cases an ulcer
do_now: Move the animal into shade and keep flies away from the eyes
Do not rub or put anything in the eye; call a vet promptly, because untreated eye ulcers can cause blindness
Separate affected animals; pinkeye spreads between animals by flies and contact
prevention: Fly control
Avoid dusty feed and tall rough pasture seed heads
diseases.see_vet: A vet should examine the eye and decide on treatment.

diseases.label: swollen_udder
diseases.title: Swollen udder (suspected mastitis)
signs: Hot, hard, swollen or painful udder quarter; the animal may kick when touched
Clots, flakes, watery or bloody milk; fever and loss of appetite in severe cases
do_now: Call a vet the same day: severe mastitis can be life-threatening
Milk the affected quarter out gently and often, last, with clean hands; keep this milk away from people, calves and the bulk tank
Wash and dry the udder; keep bedding clean and dry
Do not give any medicine unless a vet instructs you; treated animals have milk and meat withdrawal periods
prevention: Clean, dry bedding and milking hygiene
Dry-cow management and regular udder checks
diseases.see_vet: Treatment depends on the cause and must follow veterinary advice.

diseases.label: nasal_discharge
diseases.title: Nasal discharge (possible respiratory infection)
signs: Runny nose (clear, thick or pus-like), coughing, fast or laboured breathing, fever
Reduced appetite, standing apart from the herd
do_now: Separate the animal in a clean, well-ventilated but draught-free place with shade, water and feed
Call a vet the same day if breathing is laboured, there is fever, or several animals are affected
Several animals with nasal discharge, mouth sores or sudden deaths can mean a notifiable disease: tell the animal-health authority
prevention: Good ventilation and low stocking density
Vaccination and parasite control as advised by a vet
diseases.see_vet: Cause and treatment need a veterinary diagnosis.

diseases.label: poor_body_condition
diseases.title: Poor body condition
signs: Visible ribs, hips and backbone, sunken flanks, dull coat, weakness
Can come from poor feed or water, worms and other parasites, or chronic disease
do_now: Check the quality and quantity of feed and clean water first
Ask a vet or animal-health worker about worms, tick-borne disease and other chronic causes, and about deworming that is approved locally
Separate very weak animals so they can feed without competition
prevention: Balanced feeding and mineral supply
Regular parasite control as advised by a vet
diseases.see_vet: If an animal stays thin despite good feed, a vet should find the cause.

diseases.label: healthy
diseases.title: No disease detected
signs: The model found nothing it recognises as one of its conditions in this photo
This does NOT prove the animal is healthy: the model only knows a few conditions and only sees what is in the photo
do_now: If the animal still seems unwell (not eating, fever, limping, discharge), contact a vet regardless of this result
Retake the photo closer, in good light, showing the affected area, and try again
prevention: Routine vaccination, parasite control and clean housing as advised by your vet
diseases.see_vet: When in doubt, ask a vet.
